issues.item: Avoid Night: Going out at night or being outside after dark
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Night' implies fear linked to darkness/outdoor danger, but there are no Threat items and no memory/trigger content tied to night-time, darkness, or outdoor contexts. For this relief-worker trauma, that strategy is not impossible, but in this profile it is the least coherent item because it addresses a threat context not otherwise represented across Triggers, Memory, or Negative Appraisals.

issues.explanation: The formulation isolates Threat completely: all edges to and from Threat are inactive. Yet the selected Threat items are central, high-intensity PTSD threat responses and are also mirrored elsewhere. This makes Threat functionally active in a way that contradicts the formulation structure.

issues.explanation: Threat: Flashbacks and Threat: Physical Reactivity are tightly linked to the Memory and Triggers nodes, but the formulation specifies no active links involving Threat. Including these as Threat items makes the profile inconsistent with the stated node architecture.

issues.item: Threat: Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
issues.explanation: Negative Appraisals: Hypervigilance and Maladaptive Strategies: Checking Surroundings both imply an ongoing current-danger/threat monitoring pattern, which again makes Threat clinically central despite Threat being fully disconnected in the formulation.

The remaining items focus on moral reminders and nightmare residue, while appraisals and strategies emphasize vigilance, rage, and fear of losing control. Entrapment could occur, but here it lacks a clear connection to the rest of the selected content and weakens coherence.

The cognitive formulation isolates Threat completely: all edges to and from Threat are inactive. However, the selected Threat items describe a prominent, connected threat response cluster (flashbacks, strong physical reactivity, concentration problems from reminders), which is difficult to reconcile with a formulation in which Threat has no active links to Triggers, Memory, Negative Appraisals, or Maladaptive Strategies.

The Threat node is clinically misaligned with the formulation: all incoming and outgoing Threat edges are inactive, so Threat should be relatively isolated or not central. However, the selected threat items describe an active symptomatic threat response cluster (strong emotional/physical reactivity and concentration disruption) that appears tightly tied to triggers and memory intrusions. This creates a contradiction with the formulation structure, especially given concurrent trigger and memory items that imply exactly the kind of reminder-linked threat activation the model marks as inactive. The other nodes are broadly coherent with each other and with the trauma type.

The Threat node is clinically incoherent with the provided cognitive formulation. Threat has no active incoming or outgoing edges, so it should not appear as a tightly integrated maintaining component. Yet all three selected Threat items are non-specific PTSD symptom/severity indicators rather than a coherent sense of current threat, and they are not meaningfully linked to the active Triggers, Memory, Negative Appraisals, and Maladaptive Strategies pattern.

Threat is structurally isolated in the formulation, but 'Scanning for Danger' is tightly mirrored by both Maladaptive Strategies: 'Checking Surroundings' and Negative Appraisals: 'I have to be on guard all the time,' making threat function as an active linked node rather than an isolated one.

Negative Appraisals: 'I have to be on guard all the time' overlaps almost exactly with Threat: 'Scanning for Danger' and Maladaptive Strategies: 'Checking Surroundings,' which contradicts the formulation because Threat has no active links to or from these nodes.

Threat: 'Negative Emotions' is very broad and non-specific, while the rest of the profile centers on intrusive reliving, moral/entrapment triggers, and vigilance-based coping; as a Threat item it does not fit the otherwise isolated, weakly integrated role of threat in this formulation.

vignette: Decades had passed since Thien left the campaign behind, but the past did not remain in its proper place. During those years as a relief worker, the landscape was defined by sudden moral fractures and the crushing weight of having no viable route forward. He stood amid collapsing aid depots and watched colleagues prioritize their own safety over protocol, while escape routes narrowed until every direction felt blocked. Time moved forward, yet his mind refused to archive the footage. When he sat at his home desk parsing complex datasets, the screen's glow would occasionally slip, and the memories would arrive with the same breathless immediacy. They played across his attention like a looped film, each frame arriving with the full, unfiltered weight of that time. He felt the dust and the heat in his own chest, certain he was standing in those streets again rather than recalling them. The repetition never paused. Now eighty, Thien's days unfolded in a quiet study surrounded by monitors and server racks. His body spent most hours braced, shoulders tight, muscles coiled and ready to snap toward any movement. When he reviewed volunteer logs or watched community reports, he noticed people acting with selfish disregard, and a cold spike of horror and guilt would flood his system. He was certain the world was fundamentally unsafe, that the ground could give way without warning. The physical tension rarely eased. He carried the thought that his own reactions signaled he was going crazy. He watched his own temper with equal dread, certain that if he lost his restraint, he would not be able to control his anger and would do something terrible. Fear, shame, and anger often sat heavy in his throat, coexisting with the constant readiness of his frame. Thien navigated these overlapping experiences by building quiet habits. He kept his digital feeds muted whenever articles mentioned distant conflicts or humanitarian crises, turning away from the reports that mirrored his past. Before joining any video call or stepping into a university lab meeting, he rehearsed his opening lines in the stillness of his study, running through phrases until they felt steady. He checked his surroundings every time he entered a room, his eyes tracing doorways, windows, and corners for any sign of danger. These patterns had quietly reshaped his weeks. He had stopped attending field briefings. The idea of being cornered in a crowded room sat heavily with him. He canceled weekend dinners with his children and grandchildren. He could not bear the thought of being trapped in a bustling restaurant with no way to slip away. The distance had grown between him and the people he loved, sitting side by side in the same quiet house. Sleep offered no pause. When he finally drifted off, the film resumed, and he woke gasping, the residual terror of the dream clinging to his skin for hours. The transition from dark to dawn left him shuddering, the negative emotions lingering long after his eyes adjusted to the morning light. He sat at his desk for years, methodical and precise, but the data no longer felt like a refuge. The constant alertness, the replaying, the careful distance he kept from news and from unpredictable social spaces-it had grown too heavy to carry alone. He finally booked an appointment because he no longer trusted his own hands to steady the work he valued, and he feared the moment he would finally lose control of what he carried. What he hoped for, quietly, was a way to let the film stop, to stop bracing for a strike that did not come, and to walk through a room without scanning the doors.
